subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Expected Utility: The Old Model
description: A micro-lesson that makes Expected Utility: The Old Model usable.

hook.text: For 300 years, economists assumed people weigh costs and benefits like calculators. They don't.

buildup.text: Expected utility theory says a rational person always picks the option with the highest expected value.

discovery.text: Bernoulli proposed this in 1738. It works on paper. But people routinely violate it in experiments.

twist.text: Allais showed people prefer a sure $1 million over a gamble worth more in expected value. We're not calculators.

climax.text: Expected utility describes how people should decide. Prospect theory describes how they actually do.

punchline.text: Rationality is a theory. Behavior is the data.

quiz.question: What did Allais's paradox reveal?
options: People prefer sure gains over higher-value gambles
Expected utility theory was never useful

details.summary: Expected utility theory assumes people make rational decisions by multiplying each outcome's probability by its utility and choosing the option with the highest expected value. Prospect theory emerged because real human behavior systematically violates this model.
details.whyItMatters: Expected utility was the foundation of economics for decades, but it cannot explain why people buy insurance and lottery tickets simultaneously. Its failures motivated Kahneman and Tversky to develop prospect theory.
takeaways: Expected utility assumes rational probability-weighted decision making
Real decisions systematically deviate from expected utility predictions
The Allais Paradox was an early demonstration of expected utility's failures

faq.question: What is the Allais Paradox?
faq.answer: Maurice Allais showed that people prefer a certain $1 million over a gamble with higher expected value, but reverse their preference in a mathematically equivalent choice. This violated expected utility's consistency axiom and embarrassed the field.

faq.question: Is expected utility theory completely wrong?
faq.answer: Not entirely. It works reasonably well for simple, repeated decisions with clear probabilities. But for one-time, emotional, or complex decisions, prospect theory captures human behavior far more accurately.
